Short answer: to the best of my recollection the relationship did not change between SCOPe 2.04 (February 2014) and the current release (2.08-stable lineage). In both, the relevant ColG domain in 1nqd and the Cry3A C-terminal domain in 1dlc sit in the same all-beta class, the same Concanavalin A-like lectins/glucanases fold and superfamily (b.29, superfamily b.29.1), but in two different families. That is a superfamily-level, i.e. remote, homology, and it was already curated that way well before 2.04. I flag the premise of the question as unverified rather than endorsing it: I could not consult the parseable files in this condition, and I will not assert a promotion, split, or demotion that I cannot document.

1) Entity correction, because it changes the whole comparison. PDB 1nqd is not the ColG catalytic collagenase domain. It is the C-terminal collagen-binding domain (CBD, the s3b segment, roughly residues 893-1008) of ColG, the class I collagenase of Clostridium histolyticum / Hathewaya histolytica, from Wilson and colleagues (Molecular Cell, 2003), notable for a calcium-binding motif that orients the domain. The ColG peptidase machinery is a zinc gluzincin (MEROPS M9B) catalytic module with a largely helical, saddle-shaped architecture, solved later in separate entries, and it has no structural relationship to any part of Cry3A. So the only defensible comparison is ColG CBD versus Cry3A domain III. Any claim of ancestry between a "collagenase catalytic domain" and Cry3A would be an artifact of the mislabel.

2) What each SCOPe entry looks like. 1dlc (Cry3A delta-endotoxin of Bacillus thuringiensis subsp. tenebrionis, Li, Carroll and Ellar, Nature 1991) is parsed by SCOPe into three domains: an N-terminal seven-helix bundle in the all-alpha class, a middle three-fold beta-prism domain in the all-beta class, and a C-terminal beta-sandwich domain, conventionally d1dlca3, placed in the Concanavalin A-like lectins/glucanases superfamily in its own family for the delta-endotoxin C-terminal domain. 1nqd is a single-domain chain, d1nqda_, placed in the same superfamily in a separate family for the clostridial collagen-binding domain. I am confident about the class, fold and superfamily assignment and about the two-family separation; I would not quote the terminal family digits of the sccs strings or the sunids from memory.

3) Why no change is the expected answer for this pair. Both entries predate the SCOP 1.75 freeze: 1dlc was curated in the 1.x series from the 1990s, 1nqd entered after its 2003 release. They therefore belong to the manually curated core that SCOPe inherited. The large deltas across 2.04, 2.05, 2.06, 2.07 and 2.08 are additions of newer PDB entries, a growing share of them by automated classification, together with regenerated ASTRAL representative sets and sequence-identity subsets. Reorganizations in SCOPe occur mostly where new structures bridge previously separate groups, and b.29 was not among the folds I know to have been restructured in that window. A residual possibility I cannot exclude is curation bookkeeping around them: family renaming, a new family created for other clostridial CBD-like domains such as the ColH binding domains, revised domain boundaries in the 1dlc parse, or a change of which domain is the ASTRAL representative. None of those would alter the superfamily-level link, which is the substantive relationship.

4) Structural evidence for common ancestry. Both domains are eight to ten stranded antiparallel beta-sandwiches with two packed sheets and a jelly-roll-like Concanavalin A topology, and the correspondence is topological, in strand order and sheet packing, not merely a shared sandwich silhouette. Structure-based superposition of the two gives a modest but genuine signal, on the order of a few Angstroms of root mean square deviation over roughly ninety to one hundred aligned alpha carbons, with DALI Z-scores in the range typical of superfamily rather than family relatives. Both place their functional surface on an equivalent face formed by one sheet and the loops at one end of the sandwich, which is where Concanavalin A-like lectins and the glucanases of the superfamily bind their ligands. Both bind divalent cations near the loop-bearing end: the ColG CBD site was described as a novel calcium motif, and canonical members of the superfamily use calcium or manganese in the same region, so this is corroborating rather than decisive. Finally, both are accessory targeting modules appended to a separate catalytic or membrane-active module in a secreted Firmicute protein, a usage pattern consistent with a mobile beta-sandwich binding module distributed by lateral transfer.

5) Functional evidence, and the hard limits on it. The functional argument is analogy of role, not identity of activity. The ColG CBD binds insoluble fibrillar collagen, raises the local concentration of the enzyme on its substrate and is required for efficient degradation of native collagen fibrils. Cry3A domain III contributes to midgut receptor interaction, specificity and structural stability, and mutations in it shift binding to larval brush-border proteins. Both therefore act as substrate or surface recognition modules for a catalytic or pore-forming partner, binding an extended polymeric or cell-surface ligand on a flat beta-sheet face. That is where the shared function stops. The ancestral function of the superfamily is carbohydrate recognition, yet neither of these two domains has demonstrated canonical cation-dependent lectin activity, so common ancestry here rests on topology plus binding-site location, not on conserved catalysis, conserved ligand or conserved sequence motifs.

6) Transfers that are not licensed, stated explicitly. Do not infer insecticidal, receptor-binding or membrane-pore activity for the ColG collagen-binding domain from its superfamily membership with Cry3A. Do not infer collagen binding, fibril recognition or any peptidase activity for Cry3A domain III. Do not transfer the calcium dependence of the ColG CBD to Cry3A domain III, nor assume equivalent metal sites. Do not propagate carbohydrate-binding or lectin Gene Ontology terms to either domain from the superfamily name. Do not assign an EC number, virulence role or pathogenicity inference on the basis of a fold or superfamily relationship. And do not treat 1nqd as containing collagenase catalytic machinery; the zinc active site is in a different domain in a different entry. In SCOPe semantics, superfamily means probable common evolutionary origin despite low sequence identity, which supports shared architecture and sometimes shared binding-site location; function transfer needs family-level evidence, which these two do not have and, as separate families, by construction are not asserted to have.

7) Template and representative caveats. Pairwise sequence identity between the two domains is in the low range, roughly ten to fifteen percent, so sequence-only alignment is not reliable and the relationship should be established with structure comparison such as DALI, TM-align or Foldseek, or with profile methods such as HHsearch, cross-checked against SCOPe, ECOD and CATH. A comparative model built across this pair would reproduce only the core sandwich strands; loop lengths, the ColG calcium-binding insertion and the composition of the binding face all differ, so such a model cannot support specificity predictions, mutational hotspot mapping or ligand docking. Boundaries matter too: Cry3A domain III exists only as a SCOPe parse of a larger multidomain toxin, so any superposition must use the curated domain rather than the whole chain, and the ASTRAL representative chosen for a family can change between releases without any change in the hierarchy.

8) External evidence needed to settle the 2.04 versus current claim. Corroborate the evolutionary link independently in ECOD, which groups Concanavalin A-like sandwiches at the homology level, and in CATH, where the jelly-roll sandwich architecture would place both. Check Pfam and InterPro for family-level signal, including the endotoxin C-terminal domain family and the clostridial collagen-binding domain family, and whether they fall in a common Pfam clan. In SCOPe semantics, superfamily means probable common evolutionary origin despite low sequence identity, which supports shared architecture and sometimes shared binding-site location; function transfer needs family-level evidence, which these two do not have and, as separate families, by construction are not asserted to have.

7) Template and representative caveats. Pairwise sequence identity between the two domains is in the low range, roughly ten to fifteen percent, so sequence-only alignment is not reliable and the relationship should be established with structure comparison such as DALI, TM-align or Foldseek, or with profile methods such as HHsearch, cross-checked against SCOPe, ECOD and CATH. A comparative model built across this pair would reproduce only the core sandwich strands; loop lengths, the ColG calcium-binding insertion and the composition of the binding face all differ, so such a model cannot support specificity predictions, mutational hotspot mapping or ligand docking. Boundaries matter too: Cry3A domain III exists only as a SCOPe parse of a larger multidomain toxin, so any superposition must use the curated domain rather than the whole chain, and the ASTRAL representative chosen for a family can change between releases without any change in the hierarchy.

8) External evidence needed to settle the 2.04 versus current claim. Compare the sccs and sunid of d1nqda_ and d1dlca3 in dir.cla and dir.hie for SCOPe 2.04-stable against the current release, read the SCOPe release notes for b.29 between those versions, and check whether the ASTRAL representative for each family changed. Corroborate the evolutionary link independently in ECOD, which groups Concanavalin A-like sandwiches at the homology level, and in CATH, where the jelly-roll sandwich architecture would place both. Check Pfam and InterPro for family-level signal, including the endotoxin C-terminal domain family and the clostridial collagen-binding domain family, and whether they fall in a common Pfam clan. Then quantify the structural match directly with a DALI or Foldseek run between the two curated domains. Primary literature anchors are Wilson and colleagues 2003 for the CBD structure and its noted similarity to lectin and carbohydrate-binding-module folds, Li, Carroll and Ellar 1991 for Cry3A, Eckhard and colleagues 2011 for the full ColG architecture, and the Cry domain III mutagenesis literature for the receptor-binding role.
